title: Budapest Castle Hill
subtitle: A walk through what was destroyed and what was rebuilt on the Buda plateau
intro: This is the medieval core of Buda, on a limestone plateau above the Danube. Almost nothing you see is untouched: the district was wrecked in the 1686 siege that ended Ottoman rule and again in the 1944-1945 siege, and most of what stands is 19th- and 20th-century reconstruction over medieval foundations. This tour points out which parts are genuinely old, which are careful re-creation, and which are outright modern.

practical.start: The lower station of the Castle Hill Funicular on Clark Ádám tér, at the Buda end of the Széchenyi Chain Bridge. Ride up or use the stairs beside the track.
practical.end: The Vienna Gate (Bécsi kapu) at the north end of the district, on Bécsi kapu tér.
practical.terrain: A steep climb from the river (funicular or roughly 15 minutes of steps). The plateau itself is fairly level but paved almost entirely in cobbles and setts, which are hard going for wheels and heels. Bastion walkways and the western promenade have steps; a few modern lifts exist on the wall circuit. Wheelchair users can manage the main streets with effort but should expect rough surfaces and some blocked sightlines at the ramparts.
practical.best_time: Early morning. The crowds at Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion build through the day, the upper Fisherman's Bastion terraces are free before the ticket booth opens, and the morning light falls on Pest across the river.

stops.name: Castle Hill Funicular
stops.stand_here: At the lower station on Clark Ádám tér, facing up the track toward the hill.
stops.text: You are looking at a working piece of 1870 engineering, or rather a faithful copy of one. The line opened on 2 March 1870, built at the suggestion of Count Ödön Széchenyi to carry officials and residents up the steep hill; it is often described as the second funicular in Europe. The original cars were wooden and steam-hauled from the lower station. Bombing in the 1944-1945 siege destroyed the cars and both terminals, and the wreck sat unused for four decades. What runs today dates from a reconstruction that reopened on the line in 1986: the two stepped cars are replicas, the machinery is electric, and the glass terminal buildings are modern. The two pedestrian bridges crossing the track were part of the original layout, removed in 1900 and rebuilt to the old design in 1983. It is a short ride, a 95 m line rising about 50 m at a maximum incline of 31.75 degrees, and the point of it is the view back over the river rather than the distance covered.
look_for: the stepped, terraced profile of the two cars
the two footbridges spanning the track
the modern glass upper terminal against the palace wall
stops.next: Ride or climb to the top. Leave the upper station and walk south a short way onto the palace forecourt and Szent György tér; the palace mass is ahead of you.

stops.name: Buda Castle (Royal Palace)
stops.stand_here: On the palace forecourt near the top of the funicular, facing the long neo-Baroque wing and its dome.
stops.text: The palace looks continuous and old and is neither. A royal residence has stood here since the medieval kings, but the building in front of you is essentially a late 19th-century creation twice remade. Miklós Ybl began a large expansion in 1890; after his death Alajos Hauszmann took over and gave the palace its neo-Baroque form, finished by 1905. The 1944-1945 siege gutted it: the dome and roofs were broken, fires burned unchecked for want of water, and the interiors were lost. The postwar reconstruction of the 1950s and 1960s rebuilt the shell but stripped Hauszmann's ornament and replaced his tall neo-Baroque dome with the plainer one you see now, turning the palace into museums. Since 2019 the National Hauszmann Program has been partly re-reconstructing the pre-war palace: the Riding Hall, the Guardhouse and St Stephen's Hall have been rebuilt, the last reopened in August 2021. So you are looking at three layers at once: Hauszmann's design, the communist-era simplification, and a current attempt to undo it.
look_for: the plainer postwar dome, not Hauszmann's original
the crisp new stonework of recently rebuilt wings
the bronze Turul bird on the terrace railing
stops.dates: Hauszmann rebuild to 1905; postwar reconstruction 1950s-60s; Hauszmann Program from 2019
stops.next: Walk north out of the palace zone through Szent György tér and Dísz tér, then continue into Tárnok utca. Stop at the corner house numbered 18, on your left.

stops.name: Golden Eagle Pharmacy
stops.stand_here: On the pavement of Tárnok utca in front of number 18, at the corner with Anna utca.
stops.text: This corner house is more interesting than its calm classical front admits. It is a two-storey burgher's house built at the start of the 18th century on the remains of a medieval trading house, and the plain facade you see was reworked in classicist style around 1820, keeping the older Baroque statue niche. The rebuild after the medieval ruins was carried out at the behest of Lorenz Rieger, chief physician of the Buda garrison; in 1745 it passed to the pharmacist Joseph Rettig, and the Town Pharmacy operated at this address until 1910. After the 1944-1945 siege the ground-floor rooms were restored specifically to house a pharmacy-history exhibition, which is why the interior now reads as a period apothecary rather than a shop. The Golden Eagle name belongs to the institution, which was the first pharmacy in Buda after the Ottomans were expelled and moved several times before settling here. Look at the base of the wall and the door surrounds for the medieval and 18th-century stonework left exposed.
look_for: the Baroque statue niche kept in the later facade
the carved stone door surround
the wrought shop sign on the corner
stops.dates: medieval core; rebuilt early 18th c; facade c. 1820; pharmacy here to 1910
stops.next: Continue north; Tárnok utca opens into Szentháromság tér. First stop at the three-fronted building on the left, at the corner where Szentháromság utca meets the square.

stops.name: Old Buda Town Hall
stops.stand_here: At the corner of the square and Úri utca, looking up at the corner oriel with the statue in its niche.
stops.text: This was the seat of the town of Buda, and it is one of the more genuinely early-18th-century buildings on the hill. Work on it began around 1700 (sources give either 1692 or 1702) on the remains of smaller medieval houses, directed by the Italian master Venerio Ceresola, who sat on the Buda council himself; that explains the Italian Baroque of the front. The reliefs on the closed corner oriel were modelled by his compatriot Francesco Giuseppe Barbieri. The council held its first meeting here on 6 June 1710. The upper floor of the Úri utca wing was added only in 1774, to plans by Máté Nepauer, and the little bell-and-clock turret dates from 1818. In the niche at the corner facing Szentháromság tér stands Pallas Athene, carved by the Italian sculptor Carlo Adami in 1785, holding a shield with the arms of Buda. The building served as Buda's town hall until 1873, when Buda, Óbuda and Pest merged into Budapest. Inside the gateway, medieval seat-niches survive.
look_for: the Pallas Athene statue with Buda's arms on its shield
the two carved corner oriels on stone brackets
the small bell and clock turret of 1818
stops.dates: begun c. 1700; first council meeting 1710; Athene statue 1785
stops.next: Turn a few steps west into Úri utca to the small widening where the equestrian statue stands.

stops.name: Equestrian Statue of András Hadik
stops.stand_here: At the junction of Úri utca and Szentháromság utca, facing the mounted figure.
stops.text: A bronze hussar general on a rearing stallion, this is also a regimental memorial. It was unveiled on 29 April 1937, the work of the sculptor György Vastagh the Younger, cast in bronze on a limestone pedestal. It commemorates András Hadik, an 18th-century field marshal under Maria Theresa and once commandant of Buda Castle, and doubles as the monument to the 3rd Hussars, whose fallen from 1702 onward are listed in a glass case set into the plinth. Hadik's fame rests partly on a raid of October 1757, when he led a light cavalry force to the gates of Berlin and levied a ransom before withdrawing. Note the polished patch on the horse. A superstition among students of the Budapest University of Technology holds that rubbing the stallion's testicles brings luck in examinations, and enough hands have done so that the bronze there is worn bright against the darker surface of the rest. The gesture is much repeated by guides; the luck is not documented.
look_for: the bright-worn bronze between the horse's hind legs
the glass case of regimental names in the pedestal
the detailed Baroque uniform and harness
stops.next: Walk north up Úri utca. Look into the gateways of the older houses as you pass; stop at number 24 on your right.

stops.name: Úri utca and its medieval seat-niches
stops.stand_here: In the vaulted gateway of Úri utca 24, looking at the stone benches recessed into both side walls.
stops.text: These are the most genuinely medieval things you can see in the district, and most people walk straight past them. In the barrel-vaulted entrance passages of many houses along Úri utca and Országház utca, Gothic seat-niches (ülőfülkék) are cut into both side walls, pointed stone recesses with plain benches. The house at number 24 goes back to the 14th century and keeps a row of them, with five different stonemasons' marks carved on the northern side. Comparable niches survive at number 6, where the passage of a medieval cloth merchant's house is nearly all that came through the 1944-1945 siege, and at number 31, one of the few houses where the medieval detail could be fully excavated and restored after the war. What the niches were for is not settled; a common suggestion is that merchants used them to lay out and measure cloth. Unlike most of the district's medieval look, these are original fabric, not reconstruction. Step in far enough to see the benches are cut into the living wall, not applied.
look_for: pointed Gothic niches on both walls of the passage
stonemasons' marks incised in the stone
the barrel vault of the entrance passage
stops.next: Return to Szentháromság tér. In the centre of the square stands the tall Baroque column.

stops.name: Holy Trinity Column
stops.stand_here: On the south side of the column, where the reliefs on the pedestal face you.
stops.text: This is a plague column, a votive monument of a kind put up across Catholic central Europe after epidemics. The one you see is the second on the spot: an earlier column of 1706 was moved away, and after a fresh outbreak the town commissioned a larger one. It was built between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713, the work of the sculptor Fülöp Ungleich, with the reliefs and coats of arms carved by Antal Hörger. It stands about 14 metres high on a stepped hexagonal base. The Holy Trinity crowns the pillar; below are saints associated with plague and intercession, and three pedestal reliefs, one showing King David praying for the plague to end, one the epidemic raging with the castle behind, and one the building of the monument itself. Some of the weathered figures were recarved and the originals moved to museum store, so parts of what you see are copies. The imperial eagle was cut from one shield in the 19th century and replaced in 1967 by a text recording a restoration.
look_for: the three narrative reliefs at pedestal level
the shields with the arms of Hungary and Buda
the Trinity group at the very top
stops.next: The large church directly to the north-east is Matthias Church. Walk to its main west front.

stops.name: Matthias Church
stops.stand_here: In front of the south tower, on Szentháromság tér, looking up the tower and along the tiled roof.
stops.text: Properly the Church of Our Lady, this is the most thoroughly reimagined building on the hill. There has been a church here since the 13th century (documents of 1255 and 1269), rebuilt as a hall church under King Sigismund in the 15th century, with the south tower begun under King Matthias, whose name the church now carries. The Ottomans used it as a mosque; the 18th century gave it a Baroque interior. What you see is the reconstruction Frigyes Schulek carried out between 1874 and 1896: he stripped the Baroque, excavated the medieval fragments, and rebuilt the church toward an idealised Gothic state, inventing detail where evidence was missing. The south (Matthias) tower, 78.16 metres, was largely rebuilt by him, and the diamond-patterned roof carries nearly 150,000 glazed Zsolnay tiles. How much true medieval fabric survives underneath is argued about; Schulek is generally credited with keeping what he could, but the building is best understood as a scholarly Gothic re-creation rather than a medieval survival. It was damaged again in 1945 and restored, and worked on once more between 2004 and 2014.
look_for: the Zsolnay ceramic tiles of the roof
the largely rebuilt south (Matthias) tower
reused medieval carved fragments around the portals
stops.next: Walk behind the church to the east, to the white terraces and turrets overlooking the Danube.

stops.name: Fisherman's Bastion
stops.stand_here: On the lower terrace looking up at the linked white turrets, with the river behind you.
stops.text: This never defended anything. Despite the battlements and turrets, it was built between 1895 and 1902 as a decorative viewing terrace, designed by Frigyes Schulek to set off the church he had just rebuilt and to dress up this stretch of the old wall for Hungary's millennium celebrations. It stands on the line of the medieval city wall. A consensus among historians holds that in the Middle Ages this part of the wall was protected by the guild of fishermen, who lived under the walls in the so-called Fishtown or Watertown, which is where the name comes from. The style is neo-Romanesque, chosen to evoke the era around the year 1000. The seven main turrets stand for the seven Magyar tribes said to have settled the Carpathian Basin in 895. The equestrian statue of King Stephen nearby is by Alajos Stróbl, from 1906. It is honest architecture in the sense that it makes no serious pretence of being a fortress: the arcades, benches, windows and open galleries are those of a promenade, not a rampart. The lower terraces are free; the upper towers carry a small charge in season.
look_for: the seven conical turrets for the seven tribes
the open arcades and stone benches of a promenade
the Stephen I equestrian statue of 1906
stops.next: Walk north to Hess András tér, past the north side of the church. On the far side, built into the Hilton hotel, are the exposed ruins and a stone tower.

stops.name: Dominican Monastery of St Nicholas (ruins)
stops.stand_here: On Hess András tér, facing the stub of stone tower and the ruined walls set between the two blocks of the Hilton hotel.
stops.text: The blank-looking stone tower and the wall fragments wedged into the hotel are the remains of a Dominican friary. The order settled in Buda under King Béla IV, and the community was established enough to hold a general chapter of the order here in 1254; the church stood on an earlier chapel site. The tall St Nicholas tower was built in the first half of the 15th century and was one of the district's landmark structures. The friary decayed through the Ottoman period, used as stables and stores, and the site was later built over. When the Hilton was planned, the ground was excavated in a long campaign through the 1960s and 1970s, and the architect János Sedlmayr designed the preserved ruins into the new hotel, which opened on 31 December 1976: the tower, the church wall and the cloister court were kept, and the medieval detail is a mix of surviving stone and conservation work. The exact dating of parts of the complex is debated. In the former apse stands a 1937 statue of the friars Julianus and Gerhardus, moved here when the hotel was built.
look_for: the truncated St Nicholas tower
the ruined church wall dividing the hotel
the Julianus and Gerhardus bronze in the old apse
stops.next: Continue north across the square to the classical-fronted corner house with a small red relief on its facade, at Hess András tér 3.

stops.name: Red Hedgehog House
stops.stand_here: On Hess András tér in front of number 3, looking up at the relief in the panel beneath the central first-floor window.
stops.text: This corner house is said to be the oldest dwelling in Budapest still in continuous use. It was formed in the 18th century by merging three or four separate medieval houses, the oldest parts going back to around the second half of the 13th century; in the 14th century one owner was the palatine Miklós Kont. It later ran as an inn called Zum Roten Igel, the Red Hedgehog, and was used for balls and for some of the earliest theatre performances in Buda. The classical face you see comes from a remodelling around 1810, and the small painted relief of a red hedgehog, the inn's sign, was placed on the facade in 1820. It took only minor damage in 1944-1945, and it was as the fallen plaster came away that medieval fragments reappeared. On the sides you can read the seams: the Táncsics Mihály utca elevation shows the joins between the old separate houses, with a patch of late-medieval ashlar pattern and a medieval window opening left exposed among the classical work.
look_for: the small red hedgehog relief under the central window
the exposed medieval window and ashlar on the Táncsics utca side
the classical door and shopfronts of the c. 1810 remodelling
stops.dates: medieval core; classicist remodelling c. 1810; hedgehog relief 1820
stops.next: Walk west across the district to the Tóth Árpád promenade on the western rampart. Turn left (south) along the wall a short way to the round bastion carrying a bronze horseman.

stops.name: Veli bej Tower
stops.stand_here: On the Tóth Árpád promenade beside the round bastion that carries the bronze equestrian monument.
stops.text: This round bastion in the western wall is Ottoman work, one of a series the Turks built or reshaped along this side of the fortress. The usual dating is around 1570, though the sources hedge it, and it is named after Veli bej, who was sanjak-bey of Hatvan under the Buda governor Sokollu Mustafa and financed building in the town; note that he was a bey, not a pasha, so the label often given to these towers is loose. It originally held casemates, vaulted gun chambers, inside. Unlike some of its neighbours it is not recorded as having been demolished and rebuilt, so comparatively more of the fabric here is genuinely 16th-century, though no source quantifies how much. What draws the eye now is the bronze on top: the memorial to the Transylvanian 2nd Hussars by Lajos Petri, a rearing horse with a bugler, put here in the 1930s. Set the antiquarian Turkish name aside and what you are standing on is a genuine piece of the Ottoman fortress, reused as a plinth.
look_for: the curved masonry of the round bastion
the bronze hussar on the rearing horse above
the drop to the west and traces of the outer wall line
stops.next: Walk north along the promenade. Where the wall turns, drop down to Kapisztrán tér; the tall stone tower standing alone in the square is your next stop.

stops.name: Mary Magdalene Tower
stops.stand_here: On Kapisztrán tér, at the foot of the free-standing tower, where the outline of the vanished church is marked on the ground.
stops.text: This tower stands almost alone because the church it belonged to was deliberately destroyed. The Church of St Mary Magdalene began in the 13th century as the parish of the Hungarian townspeople; at the end of the 15th century it was enlarged to three aisles and this tower was built. Under Ottoman rule it was for a time the only working Christian church in the castle, shared by Catholics and Protestants until 1603, then turned into a mosque. It was largely wrecked when Buda was retaken in 1686, rebuilt in Baroque form between 1717 and 1733, made into an archive in 1786, and given to the Buda garrison as their church in 1817. The 1944-1945 siege ruined it. Rather than repair it, the communist authorities demolished the body of the church around 1950, reportedly on Rákosi's own order, keeping and conserving only the medieval tower, which they thought might draw visitors. Restoration of the tower began in 1950; it was closed for decades and reopened as a lookout in 2017. The low walls and paving around you trace where the nave stood.
look_for: the marked ground plan of the demolished nave
the late-Gothic tower standing free
the plain patched masonry from the 1950 conservation
stops.dates: medieval; church demolished c. 1950; tower kept
stops.next: Walk east along the north edge of the district to the Anjou bastion terrace, the raised gun walk between here and the Vienna Gate.

stops.name: Siavus Pasha and Murad Pasha Towers (Anjou Bastion)
stops.local_name: Sziavus pasa tornya és Murad pasa bástyája
stops.stand_here: On the Anjou bastion terrace along the north wall, looking at the two round bastion points that project from the rampart.
stops.text: This gun terrace along the north wall carries two more Ottoman bastions, and they are worth telling apart because they survive very differently. The one under you here is named for Siavus Pasha and was built between 1648 and 1650; it was largely destroyed when Buda was retaken in 1686 and lay in ruins for a long time, so how much genuine 17th-century fabric remains is uncertain. A little to the east, behind the bulk of the National Archives, is the Murad Pasha tower, built by the Buda governor Kara Murad between 1650 and 1653, with casemates inside. It was heavily damaged in 1686 too, but rebuilt in the 18th century when it was known simply as the little rondella by the Vienna Gate; its casemate was excavated in 1960 and the front restored afterwards, so much of what you see there is later work. The terrace itself was named the Anjou bastion only after 1945 and planted with its avenue of trees in 1936, for the 250th anniversary of the recapture. On the Siavus bastion stands a turbaned memorial stone to Abdurrahman Abdi, the last Ottoman governor, killed in 1686.
look_for: the two projecting round bastion points on the north wall
the turbaned Abdurrahman memorial stone ringed with chained cannonballs
the 1936 avenue of trees along the terrace
stops.next: Continue east along the terrace to the arched gateway straddling the road: the Vienna Gate.

stops.name: Vienna Gate
stops.stand_here: In front of the gate on Bécsi kapu tér, with the Lutheran church behind you and the neo-Romanesque National Archives on the north side.
stops.text: The tour ends at a gate that is younger than it looks. There has been a gate here since the Middle Ages, called the Saturday Gate for the markets held before it, and the Ottomans called it the Vienna Gate because the road to Vienna ran out through it. That medieval gate is gone. It was replaced in 1723, then by another in 1850, which was pulled down in 1896 for the millennium. The arch you walk under was built only in 1936, designed by Jenő Kismarty-Lechner from old images of the demolished gate, and put up for the 250th anniversary of the 1686 recapture of Buda; it is essentially a commemorative monument. On the castle side is a bronze angel by Béla Ohmann and a plaque marking 1686. The tall square-towered church across the square is the Lutheran Church of Budavár, designed by Mór Kallina and consecrated in 1895, its interior lost in 1945 and rebuilt without its original pulpit. The heavy neo-Romanesque block to the north is the National Archives, of the same turn-of-century decade. Taken together, this square is a good summary of the whole hill: old names, mostly modern stone.
look_for: the year 1936 and the angel relief on the castle-facing side
the dentil frieze that the medieval gate lacked
the Lutheran church tower and the National Archives across the square
stops.next: This is the end of the walk. From Bécsi kapu tér, steps and the Viennese road lead down to Széll Kálmán tér and the metro.
